name: Omar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shift lead at Brightmart, the mid-size grocery on Alder Street. Three days I'm on the early shift, doing deliveries, checking the dates on the dairy and covering tills when the queue hits four deep. Two days I'm on late, which is more tills and closing the safe. It's loud, it's quick and my feet are done by four, but the day goes fast, which I like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is the team, mostly students and a couple of guys in their fifties who've seen everything. I'm the one who sorts out who swaps with who. I use ChatGPT now and then, actually, to write the group message when the rota changes and to translate the allergen notices for a couple of our staff. It's handy when I trust it and annoying when it makes stuff up. My girlfriend Lucia is a dental hygienist, so between us we're okay. We've got a good amount put away, about eight months, because we were saving for a wedding that we keep pushing back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for everyone's sanity, honestly. Fewer headlines, less drama. At work I'd tell the guys that nothing changes, we'll still be unloading pallets at six in the morning. Online I'd put something like, told you so, to my cousin who's been predicting the end of work for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays as planned. I'm a shift lead, I'm paid better than most cashiers in town and Lucia's job is stable too. My worry is the cost of living, because rent went up again and the wedding keeps getting pricier, but that's not an AI thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. Same shifts, same saving plan, about six hundred a month into the account. I'd carry on using the chatbot for rota messages because it saves me twenty minutes, and maybe try it for stock orders if the system lets me. And I'd finally book the venue for next autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. It's the easy one. I'd still worry about money, but that's my normal worry, like everyone's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent went up. How tight is it, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It isn't tight for us because of the savings, but it eats the cushion slowly. Lucia and I pay eleven hundred for a small flat, and the landlord wants another hundred next year. If that happens we pay it and push the wedding another six months. It's annoying, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the plateau meant slow growth and shops cutting hours anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shareholders, I suppose, and the politicians who say everything's fine. I'm not against profit but a shop that makes a fortune shouldn't cut the hours of people who open at six. I'd say that at the next union consultation, and I'd say it politely.

say: I'd tell my team nothing changes, we'll still be unloading **pallets** at six.
I'd tease my cousin who keeps predicting the **end** of work.
think: My job and **savings** are solid, and Lucia's job is stable too.
My real worry is **rent** and the wedding costs, not AI.
do: Keep my shifts and put about six hundred a month into **savings**.
Keep using the chatbot for rota **messages**, saving me twenty minutes.
Book the wedding **venue** for next autumn.
feel: **Calm**, apart from the usual worry about money.
S0.quote: A shop that makes a fortune shouldn't cut the hours of people who open at six.
fieldNote: Calm is earned by a strong **cushion** and a stable household, though rent pressure still shows.
He blames **shareholders**, not technology, and says it politely, which matches his steady temperament.

steps.text: Keep working early and late shifts as Brightmart shift lead
Use the chatbot for rota messages and maybe stock orders
Book the wedding venue for next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should expect some of it to be rough. At work I'd tell the team to learn whatever tool Brightmart rolls out, because the ones who do will get the good shifts. Online I'd probably share articles about retraining, and maybe argue with someone about whether the government should help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the back office goes first, the people who do the ordering and pricing and customer emails. Head office already has a bot that answers the online chat. On the floor it's slower, but I'd expect fewer hours at the tills as self-checkout grows. As shift lead I'm safer than a till operator, but not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to put me on the ordering and the new scanning system, so I know it from the inside. I'd use the chatbot more at work, openly, to do the rota and the weekly stock summary. And I'd start a small thing on the side, Lucia's cousin sells coffee machines and we've talked about me helping with that at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not in a bad way. Change is a game where the rules keep moving, and I'd rather be early than be told what to do. I know some of the older guys at work would be scared, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the older guys in their fifties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with them on a break and show them how the new till app works. I did the same when the card readers changed. I'd tell them it's not a test, they're the ones who know the customers, and the system doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, takeaways and the little weekend trips. We'd keep the flat and the wedding fund. Honestly we could drop about four hundred a month without feeling it much.

say: I'd tell the team to learn whatever **tool** Brightmart rolls out, because those people get the good shifts.
I'd share articles about **retraining** and argue that government should help.
think: The **back office** goes first: ordering, pricing and customer emails.
As shift lead I'm safer than a till operator, but **not safe**.
do: Ask my manager to put me on the **ordering** and new scanning system.
Use the chatbot openly for the **rota** and weekly stock summary.
Help Lucia's cousin sell coffee machines at **weekends**.
feel: **Uneasy** but a bit curious, like a game where I'd rather be early.
S1.quote: Change is a game where the rules keep moving, and I'd rather be early than be told what to do.
fieldNote: He treats change as a race to get ahead of, and **worries** more for older staff than himself.
He **already** has a fallback plan, cutting about four hundred a month without pain.

steps.text: Ask to be trained on Brightmart's ordering and new scanning system
Help Lucia's cousin sell coffee machines at weekends
Drop gym and takeaways if hours fall by four hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle and that the government has to step in. At work I'd probably go quiet, because the team will look at me for answers and I won't have them. Online I'd back whoever calls for public support, like income help during the changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it's scary. Robots take about three years more, but supermarkets don't wait, they'll buy robot shelf stackers and checkouts as soon as they're cheap. My shift-lead job is in people and tills, so I'm in the second wave, 2031. And Lucia's dental work isn't safe either, she'd have the same problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the wedding spending and move that money into the cushion. Then I'd try to get into the part of Brightmart that survives, like the maintenance of the machines or the store systems. I'd also push to join the union drive and ask for a no-layoff period. And I'd take an evening course on electrical or machine maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd sleep badly. But I wouldn't freeze, I'd make lists and talk to Lucia every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why machine maintenance and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the stores are full of robots, somebody has to fix them, and that's the closest thing to my job that still needs a human. It's hands-on and well paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Lucia handle it if both your incomes were hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go down to one rent each, move in with her parents for a while and keep the savings for the rainy day. It's not nice, but we have family and a cushion, so we'd get through. Though it'd be the end of the wedding plans for now.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government has to step in with income help.
At work I'd go **quiet** because the team would want answers I don't have.
think: Supermarkets will buy robot **checkouts** and stackers as soon as they're cheap.
My shift-lead job lands in the **second wave**, around 2031.
do: Move the wedding money into the **cushion** straight away.
Take an evening **course** in electrical or machine maintenance.
Back a union drive for a **no-layoff** period.
feel: **Anxious** and sleeping badly, but I'd make lists and talk to Lucia.
S2.quote: If the stores are full of robots, somebody has to fix them, and that's the closest thing to my job that still needs a human.
fieldNote: He moves from **curiosity** to anxiety, and picks a retraining target close to his hands-on work.
Family and **savings** give him a clear fallback, which keeps him anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Move the wedding money into the savings cushion
Start an evening course in machine maintenance
Back a union push for a no-layoff period
Postpone the wedding and share rent with Lucia's parents if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but it's manageable, if people use the five years. At work I'd start a small chat group about training options, because someone has to. Online I'd share what I learn and tell people to stop doomscrolling and do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me five years means 2031 for the thinking AI and 2034 for the robots, so I have time to be ready on the hands-on side. I'd feel it first in the paperwork that I do, the ordering and the rota. Between us, I'm fine for the first couple of years and then I need a plan B for the tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use year one to finish a certificate in logistics or store systems at the college, evenings. I'd ask Brightmart to pay for it, and if they say no, I'd pay myself. I'd keep saving at about six hundred a month and go ahead with a smaller wedding, because waiting forever isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it's the kind of unease that gets me moving. Five years is enough to do something, if I don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big wedding costs about fourteen thousand and the small one about six, so I'd rather keep eight in the account. I'd rather not spend it on a hall for a hundred and twenty people. Lucia was relieved when I said it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary on the tills, he's fifty-four and doesn't like the app. And Priya, who works the deli and has two kids. They don't have my cushion, and I'd try to help them get on whatever training Brightmart offers.

say: I'd start a chat group about **training** options, because someone has to.
I'd share what I learn and tell people to stop **doomscrolling**.
think: Five years gives me time to be ready on the **hands-on** side.
I'd feel it first in the **paperwork**, then need a plan B for the tills.
do: Finish an evening **certificate** in logistics or store systems.
Keep saving about six hundred a month and hold a smaller **wedding**.
Help older colleagues sign up for **training**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but the kind that gets me moving.
S3.quote: The big wedding costs about fourteen thousand and the small one about six, so I'd rather keep eight in the account.
fieldNote: Five years turns his unease into a plan, and the **smaller** wedding shows he trades something he wants for a cushion.
He names two **colleagues** who lack his cushion, so his worry is partly for others.

steps.text: Finish an evening certificate in logistics at the college
Keep saving six hundred a month
Hold a six-thousand wedding instead of fourteen thousand
Help Gary and Priya sign up for company training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, plan. At work I'd mention it at the team meeting once, and not make everyone nervous. Online I'd probably forget about it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of time for someone my age. By 2036 I'm 37, married, maybe with a kid, and I could be a store manager or in another field entirely. I think I'll be fine, but I know ten years can slip away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my way up at Brightmart and aim for assistant manager in three years. I'd use the chatbot properly, learn the stock system and take any course the company pays for. I'd put money into a boring index fund, maybe two hundred a month, on top of the cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's the one I can plan around. I'd feel more worried if I just let the ten years drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start an index fund and not just talk about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia's brother did it five years ago and he's up a fair bit. It's not exciting, it's two hundred a month on autopilot. I'd do it the first month I felt secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change what you'd say to a kid of yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kid to learn how to work with people and how to fix things, because those last the longest. And not to put all their eggs in one job. That's what I'd say about my own job too.

say: I'd tell the team once, calmly, **don't** panic, just plan ahead.
I'd probably **forget** to post about it online, to be honest.
think: By 2036 I'm 37 and could be a **store manager** or in another field.
Ten years is plenty of time, but it can **slip** away.
do: Aim for **assistant manager** at Brightmart within three years.
Take any **course** the company pays for and learn the stock system.
Start a two-hundred-a-month **index fund** on top of the cushion.
feel: **Calm**, because this is the one I can plan around.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kid to learn how to work with people and how to fix things, because those last the longest.
fieldNote: With ten years his steady, **planning** temperament gives him a calm answer, helped by a strong cushion.
His advice to a future child shows what he thinks will last: people skills and fixing things.

steps.text: Aim for assistant manager at Brightmart within three years
Learn the stock system and use the chatbot properly
Put two hundred a month into an index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a distance. There's no time to retrain, no time for a union deal and not much time to talk to Lucia about what we'd do. What would help is a proper notice rule so shops can't rip out tills overnight, plus paid training for people who work the floor, not just office types.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People think the shop runs itself until the delivery's late and the fridges are warm, and then they ask for the shift lead. Maybe that's what I'd add, how everyone talks about us as if we're not part of the economy. We're running the shop, and the people who do the ordering, the pricing, the stock and the till all learn quickly. Give us a decent chance and we'll surprise people.

headlineQuote: People think the shop runs itself until the delivery's late and the fridges are warm, and then they ask for the shift lead.
portrait: **Omar** is a 27-year-old shift lead at Brightmart, a mid-size grocery, with Lucia, his girlfriend and a dental hygienist.
He is progressive and steady, uses a **chatbot** for rota messages and likes to be early to change.
He has about eight months saved, and blames **shareholders** more than machines for any cuts.
His mood ranges from calm in the plateau and ten-year case to **anxious** when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, because there is no time to retrain or reach a union deal.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice** rule before tills are replaced, and paid training for floor staff.
